title: New insights into the phylogenetic position and palaeobiogeography of Konkasaurus mahalana (Squamata: Scincoidea) from the Late Cretaceous of Madagascar
content:
Abstract
Konkasaurus mahalana is a Late Cretaceous Madagascan lizard, tentatively assigned to the family Cordylidae based mainly on mandibular and osteoderm morphology, although its fragmentary nature meant that its evolutionary affinities were never tested in a phylogenetic framework. As the oldest known Gondwanan scincoid and, possibly, the earliest crown-group cordyliform, Konkasaurus has been widely used as a calibration point in squamate evolutionary studies, despite this phylogenetic uncertainty. This study re-examines the holotype and new material using microcomputed tomography, allowing new skeletal elements to be reconstructed digitally and scored for phylogenetic and quantitative analyses. We incorporated Konkasaurus into a large morphological–molecular dataset and compared its osteoderm and mandibular shape with a broad sample of living scincoids using morphometrics. Our phylogenetic and morphometric results consistently support Konkasaurus as a gerrhosaurid and, specifically, place it within the Madagascan subfamily Zonosaurinae. Reclassifying Konkasaurus as a crown-group gerrhosaurid has major biogeographical implications. It extends the minimum age of the gerrhosaurid radiation back to the Late Cretaceous and implies that the family colonized Madagascar once, before 66 Mya. This is significantly later than the break-up of Gondwana and supports a hypothesis of over-water dispersal, making Konkasaurus the earliest known terrestrial vertebrate colonizer of Madagascar from Africa.
